title: Yitro: on eagles' wings (Exodus 19:4)
hook: "I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself"

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Yitro, the people camped before the mountain like one person with one heart. Your line was one heart. Did you name the thing you agree on? Today, the first words God speaks at Sinai. Day three hundred forty-five.

Ask someone how they got through the worst year of their life, and sometimes the answer isn't I was strong. It's: my sister moved in. My friends set up a meal schedule. My grandmother called every single night. Looking back, some people see they were carried, and didn't notice at the time. They were too busy surviving. Moses climbs the mountain. Before any commandment, before any thunder, God gives him a message for the people. And it begins by asking them to look back at how they got here.
screen: `HOW DID YOU GET THROUGH IT?` → `I WAS CARRIED.` → `BEFORE THE THUNDER, A MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the old Jewish translation: "Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself." Three things in one breath. What happened to Egypt. How you were carried. And where you were carried to: not to a place, but to Me. Rashi, drawing on the Mekhilta, asks: why an eagle? Other birds, he says, carry their young in their claws, because they fear the bigger birds above them. The eagle flies higher than any of them, so the only danger comes from below, from a hunter's arrow. So the eagle carries its young on its back, on its wings. Let the arrow strike me, the eagle says, rather than my children. That's the picture of God the verse is painting: a parent putting itself between the danger and the little one. The Torah uses the image again near its end, in the song of Moses in Deuteronomy, where an eagle stirs up her nest, hovers over her young, spreads her wings and carries them. A small honest note: the Hebrew word, nesher, may mean a griffon vulture as much as an eagle. Scholars debate it. Either way, it's a huge bird with a long reach. And the people the verse speaks to were carried before they knew it, through plagues and the sea and the desert, to the foot of this mountain.
screen: `WHAT I DID, HOW I BORE YOU, TO ME.` · `OTHER BIRDS CARRY IN THEIR CLAWS.` · `LET THE ARROW STRIKE ME.` · `NESHER: EAGLE, OR VULTURE?` · then, large: `ON EAGLES' WINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look back at being carried. Settle, and breathe. Think of a hard stretch in your life that's behind you now. Who carried you through it? Maybe a person, maybe several. Maybe a stranger, a teacher, a song, a community. Let their faces or their names come, one by one. Some of them you may never have thanked. If you pray, you can give thanks for them now. If not, just stay with the names, and how much of the weight was shared. The bell holds the time.
Yitro. Our portion, where God's first message at Sinai reminds the people they were carried out of Egypt on eagles' wings.
Your line: on eagles' wings. Today, tell one person who carried you through something that you noticed, even if it was years ago. Day three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers read Exodus 19:4 alongside Rashi's comment on the eagle shielding its young, and the image returns in the song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32:11.

notes: Exodus 19:4 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory (JPS 'bore', KJV 'bare'); verify exact wording and capitalization of 'Myself'.
Rashi on 19:4: eagle carries young on its wings, fearing only the arrow; 'better the arrow enter me than my children'. Confirm wording of paraphrase.
Nesher as griffon vulture: common scholarly view (e.g. based on Micah 1:16 baldness); stated as debated.
